sub_topics: Novel and unusual is petition for certiorari filed by detained Sen. Juan Ponce Enrile (JPE) in SC to obtain freedom from detention while awaiting trial
Charge: plunder and graft filed by OOO for alleged complicity in pork barrel scam
After conducting preliminary investigation (PI), OOO filed information last June 5 indicting JPE (and several others)
Having 'independently' determined existence of 'probable cause' from information and attached evidence, SBN ordered JPE's arrest and detention without bail

Unquestionably SBN followed long-standing and accepted procedure observed by all PH courts of ordering arrest and detention without bail of those charged with capital offenses (plunder, rape, murder, syndicated estafa)
Pursuant to this procedure, 'bail hearings' then immediately conducted -- prosecution required to present evidence showing evidence of guilt is 'strong'
If prosecution evidence judged 'strong', accused remains detained without bail for remainder of trial (and during appeal in case of 'guilty' verdict)
If court finds evidence 'not strong', accused released on bail while trial 'on the merits' continues to determine guilt (or innocence) and appropriate penalty

This procedure used in prosecution of all capital offenses -- including former presidents Joseph Estrada and Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo, Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Bong Revilla, and Ampatuan family members in Maguindanao massacre, who were all similarly detained without bail after arrest (or surrender)
Through counsels Estelito P. Mendoza and Eleazar B. Reyes, JPE claims this long-standing and long-revered procedure is unconstitutional and wrong
JPE reasoning from Constitution: 'In all criminal prosecutions, the accused shall be presumed innocent until the contrary is proved' (or until found guilty beyond reasonable doubt)
Charter also: 'All persons, except those charged with [capital] offenses punishable by reclusion perpetua when the evidence of guilt is strong, shall, before conviction, be bailable'
Citing jurisprudence: bail is denied in capital offenses because accused who faces probable life sentence 'has a particularly strong temptation to flee'
Analyzing these constitutional provisions and jurisprudential reason, JPE explains every person accused of any crime is constitutionally entitled to bail as general rule
As exception, bail is denied when two conditions are present: (1) evidence of guilt is strong, (2) penalty prescribed for offense is punishable by reclusion perpetua (or life imprisonment)
First condition can be determined only after prosecution finished presenting its evidence during bail hearings and after court adjudged such evidence 'strong'
Unconstitutional, illogical and wrong, JPE argues, is present procedure of detaining accused without bail PRIOR to court's ruling that evidence is indeed 'strong'
Long-standing practice puts 'the cart before the horse' and violates constitutional presumption of innocence

If SC agrees with JPE and frees him on bail, then for same reason, all those currently accused of capital offenses -- like former president Arroyo and Ampatuan family as well as Senators Revilla and Estrada -- should also be freed and granted bail while awaiting trial-court ruling on whether evidence is 'strong'

On second condition, JPE asserts in his particular case penalty would not be reclusion perpetua even if found guilty because he should be credited with mitigating circumstances of (1) old age for being over 70 years (in fact over 90) (2) voluntary surrender
Two circumstances uncontested -- without waiting to be actually arrested, JPE surrendered to authorities
Finally, JPE avers jurisprudential reason for detaining accused in capital offenses is probability of flight

In his case flight most improbable because of: (1) very old age and frail health (2) track record (in previous cases filed against him, he did not flee) (3) 'official and social standing' (senator, Cabinet member and other high government positions held from 1966 up to present), allegedly 'shows his high respect for the law'
Since JPE's petition and those of Senators Estrada and Revilla are pending in SC and therefore sub judice, CJ will refrain from making extended legal opinion
As concerned citizen, CJ will continue to monitor and report on high-profile cases especially as they relate to PNoy's daang matuwid program

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the foundational column on Sen. Juan Ponce Enrile's novel bid for bail -- the earliest Enrile-bail column in the corpus, setting up an arc that culminates in the SC's August 18, 2015 ruling granting bail (later referenced in A368, A373, A374). Novel and unusual is the petition for certiorari filed by detained Sen. Juan Ponce Enrile (JPE) in the Supreme Court to obtain his freedom from detention while awaiting his trial in connection with the charge of plunder and graft filed against him by the OOO for his alleged complicity in the pork barrel scam. After conducting a preliminary investigation, the OOO filed last June 5 an information indicting JPE (and several others) with plunder and graft. Having 'independently' determined the existence of probable cause from the information and its attached evidence, the SBN ordered JPE's arrest and detention without bail. Unquestionably, the SBN followed the long-standing and accepted procedure observed by all PH courts of ordering the arrest and detention without bail of those charged with capital offenses (like plunder, rape, murder and syndicated estafa). Pursuant to this procedure, bail hearings are then immediately conducted, in which the prosecution is required to present evidence showing that the evidence of guilt is 'strong.' If the prosecution's evidence is judged to be 'strong,' the accused shall remain in detention without bail for the remainder of the trial (and during the appeal, in case of a guilty verdict). On the other hand, if the court finds the evidence to be 'not strong,' the accused is released on bail while trial 'on the merits' continues to determine guilt (or innocence), and the appropriate penalty if eventually found guilty. This procedure is used in the prosecution of all capital offenses, like those of former presidents Joseph Estrada and Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo, Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Bong Revilla, as well as the Ampatuan family members (in the Maguindanao massacre), who were all similarly detained without bail after their arrest (or surrender). Through his counsels Estelito P. Mendoza and Eleazar B. Reyes, JPE however claims that this long-standing and long-revered procedure is unconstitutional and wrong. JPE reasons that under the Constitution, 'in all criminal prosecutions, the accused shall be presumed innocent until the contrary is proved,' or until found guilty beyond reasonable doubt; also, the Charter guarantees that 'all persons, except those charged with [capital] offenses punishable by reclusion perpetua when the evidence of guilt is strong, shall, before conviction, be bailable.' Citing jurisprudence, he adds that bail is denied in capital offenses because an accused who faces a probable life sentence 'has a particularly strong temptation to flee.' Analyzing these constitutional provisions and the jurisprudential reason for the denial of bail in capital offenses, JPE explains that every person accused of any crime is constitutionally entitled to bail as a general rule. As an exception, however, bail is denied when two conditions are present: (1) the evidence of guilt is strong, and (2) the penalty prescribed for the offense is punishable by reclusion perpetua (or life imprisonment). The first condition, he avers, can be determined only after the prosecution has finished presenting its evidence during the bail hearings and after the court has adjudged such evidence to be 'strong.' Unconstitutional, illogical and wrong, therefore, he argues, is the present procedure of detaining the accused without bail prior to the court's ruling that the evidence is indeed 'strong.' This long-standing practice, he adds, puts 'the cart before the horse' and violates the constitutional presumption of innocence. If the Supreme Court agrees with and frees him on bail, then for the same reason, all those currently accused of capital offenses -- like former president Arroyo and the Ampatuan family as well as Senators Revilla and Estrada -- should also be freed and granted bail while awaiting the ruling of the trial courts on whether the evidence of guilt in their respective cases is 'strong.' On the second condition, JPE asserts that in his particular case, the penalty to be imposed would not be reclusion perpetua even if he is found guilty, because he should be credited with the mitigating circumstances of (1) old age for being over 70 years (in fact, he is over 90) and (2) voluntary surrender. These two circumstances are uncontested -- without waiting to be actually arrested, JPE surrendered to the authorities. Finally, JPE avers that the jurisprudential reason for detaining the accused in capital offenses is the probability of flight. In his case, flight is most improbable because of (1) his very old age and frail health, (2) his track record (in previous cases filed against him, he did not flee), and (3) his 'official and social standing' (as a senator, Cabinet member and other high government positions he held from 1966 up to the present), which allegedly 'shows his high respect for the law.' Since JPE's petition and those of Senators Estrada and Revilla are pending in the Supreme Court and therefore sub judice, CJ refrains from making an extended legal opinion. However, as a concerned citizen, he will continue to monitor and report on high-profile cases especially as they relate to PNoy's daang matuwid program.
